content: 1. The Ment for Every Kid model, as discussed in Pediatrics (2011, Volume 127, Issue 4, Pages e962–970), examines the impact of this approach on pediatric primary care professionals. This study highlights the integration of mental health services into pediatric care and its implications for improving outcomes in children. 2. Feder G et al. conducted a cluster randomized trial titled Identification and Referral to Improve Safety (IRIS) to evaluate a primary care training and support program for women experiencing domestic violence. Published in The Lancet (2011, Volume 19, Pages 1788–1795), this study underscores the importance of equipping primary care providers with the skills to identify and refer victims of domestic violence effectively. 3. Garg A et al. explored strategies to enhance the management of family psychosocial problems during well-child care visits for low-income children. Their findings, published in Pediatrics (2007, Volume 120, Issue 3, Pages 547–558), emphasize the role of structured interventions in addressing psychosocial challenges in pediatric populations. 4. Grisurapong S. reviewed the health sector's responses to violence against women in Thailand, as detailed in the Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand (2004, Volume 87, Supplement 3, Pages S227–234). This work provides insights into the systemic approaches and challenges in addressing gender-based violence within the healthcare system. 5. Lo Fo Wong SLF et al. demonstrated that training programs can significantly increase awareness of intimate partner abuse among healthcare professionals. Their randomized control trial highlights the effectiveness of educational interventions in improving recognition and response to abuse. 6. McLaughlin SA et al. implemented and evaluated a training program for managing sexual assault cases in emergency departments. Published in Annals of Emergency Medicine (2007, Volume 49, Issue 4, Pages 489–494), this study underscores the importance of specialized training in improving care for sexual assault survivors. 7. Milone JM et al. investigated the impact of lectures and standardized patient encounters on medical students' acceptance of rape myths and their attitudes toward screening patients for a history of sexual assault. Their findings, published in Teaching and Learning in Medicine (2010, Volume 22, Issue 1, Pages 37–44), highlight the role of education in shaping future physicians' approaches to sensitive topics. 8. Parekh V, Currie M, and Brown CB described the development of a postgraduate sexual assault forensic medicine program, emphasizing the establishment of sexual assault medicine from the ground up. This work, published in Medicine, Science, and the Law (2005, Volume 45, Issue 2, Pages 121–128), provides a framework for training healthcare professionals in forensic medicine. 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) published the Medical Eligibility Criteria in 2010, providing evidence-based guidelines for healthcare providers to ensure safe and effective medical care. Additionally, the WHO's 2002 guidelines for medico-legal care of sexual violence survivors offer comprehensive recommendations for addressing the needs of this vulnerable population. 10. WHO/UNHCR/UNFPA developed an e-learning program in 2009 for the clinical management of rape survivors. This program, accessible online, aims to enhance healthcare providers' knowledge and skills in delivering compassionate and evidence-based care to survivors of sexual violence. 11. Coyer SM et al. examined the implementation of screening for violence against women in rural healthcare clinics. Their findings, published in the Online Journal of Rural Nursing and Health Care (2006, Volume 6, Issue 1), highlight the unique challenges and opportunities in rural settings. 12. Crandall CS and Helitzer D evaluated the impact of a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) program, as detailed in a report for the U.S. Department of Justice (Document No. 203276, December 2003). This evaluation underscores the role of SANE programs in improving care for sexual assault victims. 13. Derhammer F et al. described the use of an interdisciplinary approach in SANE programs to enhance care for sexual assault victims. Published in The Joint Commission Journal on Quality Improvement (2000, Volume 26, Issue 8, Pages 488–496), this study highlights the benefits of collaborative care models. 14. Fanslow JL, Norton RN, and Robinson EM conducted a one-year follow-up study on an emergency department protocol for abused women. Published in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health (1999, Volume 23, Issue 4, Pages 418–420), this research evaluates the long-term outcomes of such protocols. 15. Feder GS et al. conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial on the IRIS program, focusing on the identification and referral of women experiencing domestic violence. Published in The Lancet (2011, Volume 378, Issue 9805, Pages 1788–1795), this study emphasizes the importance of primary care interventions in improving safety for victims. 16. Gregory A et al. outlined the protocol for a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of the IRIS program in BMC Public Health (2010, Volume 10, Issue 1, Page 54). This protocol provides a detailed framework for evaluating the effectiveness of domestic violence interventions in primary care. 17. Harwell TS et al. reported the results of a domestic violence training program for staff at urban community health centers. Published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (1998, Volume 15, Issue 3, Pages 235–242), this study highlights the impact of training on healthcare providers' ability to address domestic violence. 18. Kim JC et al. evaluated the Refentse intervention study, which provided comprehensive care and HIV prophylaxis to sexual assault survivors in rural South Africa. Published in BMJ (2009, Volume 338, Pages 1559–1562), this study underscores the importance of integrated care models in resource-limited settings. 19. McCaw B et al. proposed a systems model approach to addressing domestic violence in a managed care setting. Published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (2001, Volume 21, Issue 3, Pages 170–176), this study highlights the need for systemic changes to improve care for victims. 20. Muñoz CF et al. evaluated the impact of a priority intervention on improving care for victims of domestic violence. Published in Atención Primaria (2001, Volume 28, Issue 4, Page 241), this study emphasizes the importance of targeted interventions in primary care. 21. Ramsden C and Bonner M provided a realistic perspective on domestic violence screening in emergency departments. Published in Accident and Emergency Nursing (2002, Volume 10, Issue 1, Pages 31–39), this study highlights the challenges and opportunities in implementing screening protocols. 22. Sampsel K et al. examined the impact of a sexual assault/domestic violence program on emergency department care. Published in the Journal of Emergency Nursing (2009, Volume 35, Issue 4, Pages 282–289), this study underscores the benefits of specialized programs in improving care for victims. 23. Spinola C et al. described the development and implementation of an intervention for addressing intimate partner violence. This work highlights the importance of evidence-based approaches in improving care for victims. 24. Feldhaus KM et al. investigated physicians' knowledge of and attitudes toward mandatory reporting laws for domestic violence. Published in Annals of Emergency Medicine (2003, Volume 41, Issue 1, Page 159), this study highlights the complexities of mandatory reporting in healthcare. 25. Gerbert B et al. conducted a qualitative analysis of how physicians with expertise in domestic violence approach the identification of victims. Published in Annals of Internal Medicine (1999, Volume 131, Issue 8, Pages 578–584), this study provides insights into best practices for identifying and supporting victims. 26. Glass N, Dearwater S, and Campbell JC evaluated intimate partner violence screening and intervention in 11 community hospital emergency departments. Published in the Journal of Emergency Nursing (2001, Volume 27, Pages 141–149), this study highlights the importance of emergency department protocols in addressing intimate partner violence. 27. Rodriguez M et al. explored patient attitudes about mandatory reporting of domestic violence and its implications for healthcare professionals. Published in the West Journal of Medicine (1998, Volume 169, Pages 337–341), this study emphasizes the need for patient-centered approaches in mandatory reporting. 28. Sachs C et al. evaluated the failure of mandatory domestic violence reporting laws to increase medical facility referrals to police. Published in Annals of Emergency Medicine (1998, Volume 31, Pages 488–494), this study highlights the limitations of mandatory reporting laws. 29. Smith JS et al. identified barriers to mandatory reporting of domestic violence encountered by nursing professionals. Published in the Journal of Trauma Nursing (2008, Volume 1, Pages 9–11), this study underscores the challenges faced by nurses in complying with reporting requirements. 30. Tilden VP et al. examined factors influencing clinicians' assessment and management of family violence. Published in the American Journal of Public Health (1994, Volume 84, Issue 4, Pages 628–633), this study highlights the complexities of addressing family violence in clinical practice. 31. Bloom SS provided a comprehensive review of monitoring and evaluating the implementation of guidelines for addressing intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women. This work emphasizes the importance of evidence-based guidelines in improving care for victims. 32. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed clinical and policy guidelines for responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women. These guidelines, prepared with input from external experts and WHO staff, provide a framework for healthcare providers to deliver compassionate and effective care to survivors.
